P1.evidence: Setter notes referenced at the open and used again mid-call — 'I think Kim also mentioned to me already that you're in quite decent shape' — which is the check working. The rep also opened by asking how to pronounce the prospect's name, then called him 'Dominic' one minute later. Frame remains three-part. Agreement asked and given, open question asked.

P2.evidence: Weight and age were both asked directly; height never was. Diet was the strongest check — meals per day, portion sizes, snack frequency, soda — and produced a clear picture. Work was asked and produced the correctional officer role, but the far more relevant fact, that he is currently not working and living on disability, only emerged forty minutes later during the money conversation and was never explored. The injury probe is notably weaker than elsewhere in this batch: the rep asked the question and got a service-connected hip injury from a convoy accident that prevents squatting, then ran no severity scale and no duration probe, which he did on nearly every other call. Health conditions were never asked — ADHD and the disability were both volunteered. Sleep was never mentioned. Energy was a running theme but never asked as a baseline.

P3.evidence: The bridge question was asked properly — 'why do you feel like, I really want to put more effort into this? Because it doesn't sound like you're in a terrible shape' — and came back thin: 'I'm like a sponge. I like soaking in stuff and learning new things.' The rep accepted that and moved on, which is the same failure as the Jimin Bhuptani call. The future-pace did work: 'let's say you get back into that old army shape, you look in the mirror, how would that be for you?' produced 'I'm in my prime again', and the rep followed with a genuinely good reframe — 'prime isn't something that was years ago, you can always decide to have a prime right now.' What was left on the table is substantial: five children, a wife who trains with him and drives him ('she looks good, so I have to look good too'), and army buddies in old photographs. None of it was turned into a why. The rep asked how old the kids were and never asked what any of this would mean for them.

P4.evidence: One well-aimed question did most of the work: 'After being out of the military, do you feel like it has been going down slowly because the workouts changed?' — which produced the whole story of bulking, sleeping in and losing the structure. The prospect then named his own gap clearly and repeatedly: 'my thing is, it's just having a workout routine. I can do all this, but I just need a routine', and later 'just being accountable... knowing that somebody's better than me is holding me accountable.' But past attempts were never framed as attempts, and P4f was never asked — which matters here more than usual, because this is a man with Army PT training who is currently mimicking free YouTube videos at the gym and already seeing results. Why he cannot build and hold a routine on his own is the entire sale and nobody asked it.

P5.evidence: The rep built a reasonable two-year picture and asked the settle question twice, rephrasing when the prospect did not understand it: 'if it stays the exact same because you don't make a change, and six months or a year from now you're still in the same place, do you feel like, yeah, it's whatever, or do you feel like no, I do really want to get to that excellence level?' The answer refused the premise entirely — 'I'm gonna still keep going... if it's six months down the road and I don't see nothing, then it's something on my end' — which is a prospect telling you he will do it with or without you. The rep did not press. That is the third call in this batch (with Geoffrey and Richard Kellis) where the settle question was deflected and the deflection was accepted, and it is the single most repeated coaching theme here.

P6.evidence: The belief check ran early and cleanly — 'Do you believe that you can get back into that old shape?' answered 'A hundred percent' — and the rep supported it well by pointing to older clients: 'if they can do it, why would you not be able to do it?' He also asked the useful non-scripted question about which of the three pillars mattered most, which produced the most revealing answer on the call. P6c is the problem: he got yeses about the programme but never a yes about investing, and the price landed on someone who demonstrably had not heard it — 'Okay. Perfect' at 00:36:53, then 'Man, $6,000, man. Good gracious' at 00:39:10. Moving to arrange a payment link on a yes that thin is what P6c exists to prevent.

P11.evidence: No agreement on either tier, so payment and onboarding were never reachable. The rep did begin the payment step prematurely, asking where to send the link, before the prospect had registered the price.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger at 00:39:10. Good moves ran: reassurance that this is what the meeting is for, then a clean won't-versus-can't isolation — 'is it absolutely not possible in the years to come, or is it more so like it's just a big chunk?' — which produced the key information, 'It's a big chunk. Like monthly, I can probably pay.' Monthly leftover was then asked and produced $150, pushed to a possible $200. Savings were asked three times and each time he explained they are ring-fenced family emergency funds. Missing: credit cards, available credit, investments, and any clean 'finances aside, nothing else keeping you from 100%' isolation. The substantive error is what followed. The prospect said he could pay monthly, and the rep never quoted the instalment option on the $6,000 that he had quoted to another prospect the previous day — he jumped straight to the $200 community tier. Even if $1,200 a month was never going to fit a $150 ceiling, the play says explore making it work before changing the product.

Gap: the prospect wants the premium specifically and rejects the substitute. 'I would just want to talk to the man myself. That's just the way I'm wired.' The downsell fails structurally here because direct human contact is the exact thing he values — he had already said the accountability pillar was what would help him most, describing Trevor as a drill sergeant and then as a father figure. Offering him a peer community instead removes the only ingredient he asked for. The rep improvised the best available answer, his own story of starting on the cheap tier because he could not afford one-on-one either, plus the credit-toward-one-on-one promise. There is no scripted route for a prospect who wants the premium, cannot afford it, and correctly identifies that the cheaper tier is not a smaller version of it.

Gap: the price did not land. He answered 'Okay. Perfect' to $6,000 and the rep proceeded to ask where to send the payment link; two minutes later it emerged he had not heard the number at all. There is no scripted confirmation step after quoting — no 'does that number work for you' or read-back — and without one a distracted or poor-connection prospect can be moved to payment on a yes that means nothing. The rep did catch it and asked directly, which is why this is partial rather than a miss.
No think-about-it from the prospect. The deferral at the end was the rep's suggestion, not the prospect's request.

The wife was raised only as a positive — a training partner who pushes him to the gym — never as an approver. He cited having a wife and five children as an affordability fact rather than a consent issue.
No timing objection; he had already started training with kettlebells and was keen to move.
No fear or doubt — 'A hundred percent. I think I can get back into it', and 'that's that army mindset that I have'.

notes: Good rapport, a well-run belief check, and one excellent question — asking which pillar would help most — that produced the most useful line in the transcript: he wants someone to hold him accountable and will treat that person like a father. Two things went wrong. The price was quoted to someone who did not hear it, and the rep was arranging a payment link before that surfaced; add a confirmation step after quoting. And when he said 'monthly, I can probably pay', the answer was a different product rather than an instalment plan on the one he wanted. Also worth reviewing for judgement rather than technique: this is a 27-year-old on disability with five children who twice explained his savings are untouchable family emergency money, and he was asked a third time.
